extracted.intended_audience: poets, painters, artists, literary critics, and writers interested in aesthetic theory of the sublime and beautiful
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for producing and evaluating sublime and beautiful effects in poetry, painting, rhetoric, and other arts — explaining which passions and techniques (terror, obscurity, imitation, sympathy, power, etc.) generate aesthetic effects. Useful for creators and critics aiming to evoke or judge strong emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society and Solitude (emotional valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society, merely as society, gives no positive pleasure in the enjoyment; absolute and entire solitude ... is as great a positive pain as can almost be conceived. Particular social enjoyments outweigh the uneasiness caused by their absence; temporary solitude is agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts between general society, particular social enjoyment, and solitude to shape emotional effects: particular company, lively conversation, and friendship produce strong pleasures; total/perpetual exclusion (absolute solitude) is intensely painful and contradicts purposes of our being. In composition choose whether to foreground companionship or solitude according to the emotional aim (contemplation vs action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy as the primary mechanism of emotional transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Sympathy is a sort of substitution, by which we are put into the place of another man, and affected in many respects as he is affected: it is by this principle chiefly that poetry, painting, and other affecting arts, transfuse their passions from one breast to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To move readers/audiences, art should enable them to 'stand in another's place' rather than rely on abstract reasoning. Sympathy can produce sublime effects (when it turns on pain/danger) or pleasures (when it turns on pleasure). Designers of tragic or affecting works should craft situations that invite sympathetic substitution (clear motives, accessible suffering) rather than argument about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight in the misfortunes of others (tragic pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a degree of delight, and that no small one, in the real misfortunes and pains of others; the delight is heightened if the sufferer is some excellent person who sinks under an unworthy fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy and historical accounts can evoke high pleasure precisely because they present grievous calamity—especially when the victim is noble/virtuous. This pleasure is mixed with uneasiness and prompts benevolent impulses; authors may exploit the blend of pity and delight but should not rely solely on the audience's knowledge of fictionality as the source of pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of tragedy depends on imitation approaching reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The nearer [a representation] approaches the reality, and the further it removes us from all idea of fiction, the more perfect is its power ... it never approaches to what it represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong tragic effect requires representations that approximate reality closely enough to suspend the audience's reflective distance; the more convincingly 'real' the imitation appears at the moment, the greater the emotional power. However, actual reality produces a stronger response than even the most elaborate imitation (example: a real execution would empty a theatre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule to distinguish power of imitation vs power of the object's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When the object represented in poetry or painting is such as we could have no desire of seeing in the reality, then I may be sure that its power in poetry or painting is owing to the power of imitation, and to no cause operating in the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this diagnostic when evaluating art: if the depicted object is one we would not wish to witness in real life (still-life of dung-hill, mean utensils), the effect arises from the artist's skilled imitation; if the object is one we'd rush to see if real, its power stems from the object's intrinsic nature rather than mere imitation. This guides genre choices (e.g., still-life vs great events) and claims about where the art's effect originates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and learning (pleasure of imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation ... prompts us to copy whatever they do; and consequently we have a pleasure in imitating, and in whatever belongs to imitation merely as it is such ... It is by imitation far more than by precept, that we learn everything; and what we learn thus, we acquire not only more effectually, but more pleasantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitative elements (style, form, gestures) in art are a source of pleasure and social cohesion; creators should recognize imitation as both a pedagogical and aesthetic force but also balance it with originality (ambition) to enable improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition and the pleasurable sense of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: God has planted in man a sense of ambition, and a satisfaction arising from the contemplation of his excelling his fellows in something deemed valuable amongst them ... it is what every man must have felt in himself upon such occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime and grand passages can produce a 'glorying and sense of inward greatness' in readers; authors may elicit this inward pride by presenting objects or language that allow readers to claim some dignity by association. Also explains social drivers like flattery and the desire to stand out—useful when crafting characters or rhetorical appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime generates astonishment by suspending the faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The passion caused by the great and sublime in nature ... is astonishment: and astonishment is that state of the soul in which all its motions are suspended, with some degree of horror ... the inferior effects are admiration, reverence, and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for astonishment (total engrossment and suspension of other thought) when seeking the highest sublime effect; lesser aims (admiration, reverence) are gradations. Structural devices that overwhelm the mind's capacities (scale, intensity, horror) help produce astonishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror as the core of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: No passion so effectually robs the mind of all its powers of acting and reasoning as fear. Whatever therefore is terrible, with regard to sight, is sublime too ... terror is in all cases whatsoever, either more openly or latently, the ruling principle of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke the sublime, incorporate elements that suggest danger or fear (not necessarily large scale): even small creatures (serpents, poisonous animals) can be sublime if conceived as dangerous. Consider combining grandeur with latent threat to maximize effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity increases dread and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: To make anything very terrible, obscurity seems in general to be necessary. When we know the full extent of any danger, when we can accustom our eyes to it, a great deal of the apprehension vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use darkness, uncertainty, vagueness, and indeterminate outlines to heighten terror and sublimity (examples: temples kept dark; Milton's descriptions of death). Avoid over-clarification—leave key elements obscure to sustain fear and awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness vs affective obscurity (obscurity often better for passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one thing to make an idea clear, and another to make it affecting to the imagination ... a great clearness helps but little towards affecting the passions, as it is in some sort an enemy to all enthusiasms whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor suggestive, crowded, confused, or indefinite imagery in poetry to move the passions more strongly than precise, clear depiction; poetry's obscurity can transport the mind toward infinity, while clear images (often painting) limit grandeur by defining bounds. Use layered, confused images to produce expansion of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power as a modification of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: I know of nothing sublime, which is not some modification of power ... the idea of vast power is extremely remote from neutral: strength, violence, pain, and terror, are ideas that rush in upon the mind together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict vast or superior power in ways that emphasize potential for harm or domination (not merely utility). Stripping strength of its dangerous capacity makes it contemptible rather than sublime (example: ox useful vs bull/battle-horse terrible). Emphasize the capacity to inflict pain or change as part of sublime imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific limits: poetry's advantage with the obscure and chimerical
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper manner of conveying the affections of the mind from one to another is by words ... a great insufficiency in all other methods of communication ... poetry, with all its obscurity, has a more general, as well as a more powerful dominion over the passions, than the other art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer verbal/poetic means when aiming to convey obscure, chimerical, or vast conceptions (apparitions, allegorical figures): poetry can assemble 'a crowd of great and confused images' that painting cannot convincingly render without risking the ludicrous. Use medium-appropriate techniques: painting relies on clearer images (though judicious obscurity helps); poetry can exploit indeterminacy to grander effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions arise more from natural constitution than from reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: I am afraid it is a practice much too common ... to attribute the cause of feelings ... to certain conclusions of the reasoning faculty ... the influence of reason in producing our passions is nothing near so extensive as it is commonly believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or crafting emotional effects, privilege physiological and instinctive mechanisms (sympathy, imitation, mechanical bodily responses) over purely rational explanations; techniques that trigger instinctive responses will be more effective than those that rely solely on argument.
